items.topic: Stage I sarcoidosis lymph node pattern recognition

actions.observe: Bilateral hilar regions for symmetric, well-defined lobulated enlargement; check right paratracheal stripe for concomitant adenopathy.
actions.when: Question asks to characterize lymphadenopathy pattern or stage sarcoidosis based on CXR findings.
actions.stop: Symmetry of hilar nodes and presence/absence of paratracheal involvement are visually confirmed.

actions.observe: Lung parenchyma for absence of focal consolidation, opacities, or fibrosis to distinguish Stage I from Stage II/III.
actions.when: Differentiating Stage I (nodes only) from advanced stages or infectious/malignant mimics.
actions.stop: Clear lung fields confirm isolated nodal disease consistent with Stage I.

items.avoid: Relying on classifier 'Mass' scores as probability or severity; assuming report generator's 'normal silhouette' negates visible hilar fullness; inferring asymmetry or calcification without direct visual confirmation.
items.source_evidence: Old model claims relied on tool outputs (classifier score 0.88 for Mass, report stating normal silhouette) which failed to capture the specific nodal pattern. Released correct answers consistently identify 'bilateral symmetric hilar lymph node enlargement' often with 'paratracheal enlargement' as key to Stage I sarcoidosis. Visual evidence in Figure 1a shows distinct bilateral hilar fullness with preserved lung fields, contradicting the generic 'normal' report and requiring direct inspection of nodal symmetry and margins rather than automated scores.

items.topic: Mass extent and displacement: inspect size and mass effect before choosing an option

actions.observe: Inspect the suspected mass boundary and how much of the hemithorax it occupies. Inspect the adjacent diaphragm, mediastinum and trachea for displacement, considering projection and visibility.
actions.when: The current question explicitly asks about a mass. Use only the current original image and all option clauses.
actions.stop: Stop when extent and displacement are observed or their uncertainty is identified; do not require a particular size, side or shift direction.

items.avoid: Do not transplant the source mass size, side, tumor type or treatment into the current case. A generic clear-lungs report or a classifier score does not settle mass extent.
items.source_evidence: Source14923 supplies a frontal radiograph and released feedback about a large lower-hemithorax mass and mass effect. The retained skill is the observable extent/displacement check, not the source diagnosis or preferred option.

items.topic: Pleural effusion presence and laterality: inspect both pleural spaces

actions.observe: Inspect each visible costophrenic angle and lateral pleural margin separately for blunting or a meniscus. Distinguish pleural fluid cues from adjacent parenchymal opacity; account for supine positioning or excluded lung bases.
actions.when: The current question explicitly concerns pleural effusion. Apply to the supplied current original image, without assuming either side is abnormal.
actions.stop: Stop after assessing each relevant side as supported, unsupported, or not assessable. Do not equate a missing angle, a negative classifier, or an inconclusive view with absence.

items.avoid: One-sided evidence cannot establish bilateral fluid. Do not copy the source lung consolidation pattern, diagnosis, or absent-fluid conclusion into the current case.
items.source_evidence: Source16691 contains a frontal source radiograph and released questions contrasting consolidation and pleural-fluid findings. The review retains the bilateral pleural-space inspection action while removing source-specific lobe, diagnosis and negative-result assertions.

items.topic: Longitudinal assessment of residual atelectasis location in resolving pneumonia

actions.observe: Compare the basal lung zones in the initial vs discharge images to identify the specific side (left vs right) where linear opacities or atelectatic streaks persist after the resolution of peripheral consolidations.
actions.when: Question asks for evolution of findings and specifies residual signs like atelectasis at a specific timepoint (e.g., discharge).
actions.stop: When the side of the residual basal opacity is visually confirmed and matched against the options.

items.avoid: Assuming bilateral symmetry in residual findings or misidentifying the side of atelectasis due to poor contrast; do not rely on classifier scores for longitudinal change.
items.source_evidence: The model previously selected 'right basal zone' for residual atelectasis, but the correct answer is 'left basal zone'. The source images (Figure 14/15 context) show that while peripheral consolidations improve, thin linear opacities remain specifically in the left base. This requires direct visual comparison of the basal regions across timepoints rather than general impression of improvement.

items.topic: Pneumothorax check: pleural line versus mimics, with original-image binding

actions.observe: Inspect the relevant apex and lateral chest for a visceral pleural line and whether lung markings extend beyond it. Consider skin folds, scapular borders and bullae as mimics. Inspect each relevant side rather than assuming the source side.
actions.when: The current question explicitly concerns pneumothorax. A single image supports only its own visible findings; temporal change requires explicitly bound prior/current originals.
actions.stop: Stop when line/marking evidence or its uncertainty is assessed for the relevant sides. Do not require pneumothorax to be present and do not infer interval change from image order.

items.avoid: Do not transfer source Figure numbers, side, timing or a positive diagnosis. Absence of a confidently seen pleural line does not prove absence when the supplied image is inadequate.
items.source_evidence: Source16844 provides paired frontal radiographs and released feedback about interval pleural-air findings. Review retains the visible line/marking check and mimic/chronology cautions, removing source figure numbers and mandatory positive findings.

items.topic: Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome vs Hypogenetic lung syndrome differentiation via hyperlucency and vascular markings

actions.observe: Compare the right hemithorax to the left for unilateral hyperlucency (increased radiolucency) and assess the density/number of pulmonary vascular markings in the hyperlucent area.
actions.when: Evaluating a patient with history of recurrent infections presenting with asymmetric lung findings.
actions.stop: When unilateral hyperlucency is confirmed alongside visibly diminished or absent pulmonary vessels on the affected side, distinguishing it from simple overinflation or effusion.

actions.observe: Inspect the hilum on the hyperlucent side for size; specifically check if it appears smaller or hypoplastic compared to the contralateral side.
actions.when: Differentiating Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome (small hilum) from Congenital Lobar Overinflation (often normal or displaced hilum) or Unilateral Absence of Pulmonary Artery.
actions.stop: Once hilar asymmetry is established in conjunction with parenchymal hyperlucency.

items.avoid: Relying on automated report generators that may hallucinate pneumothorax or atelectasis in hyperlucent lungs, or assuming 'no strong finding' from classifiers implies normality when subtle vascular paucity is present.
items.source_evidence: Old models incorrectly predicted Hypogenetic lung syndrome. The reference answer is Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome, supported by the specific combination of right hemithorax hyperlucency and vessel paucity consistent with recurrent infection history. Tool observations were unreliable (report generator claimed pneumothorax/atelectasis not supported by visual evidence of SJMS features). The key discriminant is the visual presence of hyperlucency with reduced vascularity rather than volume loss or absence of structures seen in other syndromes.

items.topic: Scimitar syndrome radiographic triad: anomalous vein, volume loss, diaphragm elevation

actions.observe: Right lower lung zone for a curvilinear tubular opacity (scimitar sign) paralleling the right heart border and descending toward the diaphragm.
actions.when: Question asks to identify findings supporting scimitar syndrome or locate the anomalous vein.
actions.stop: Curved shadow is clearly visualized adjacent to the right cardiac silhouette.

actions.observe: Right hemidiaphragm position relative to the left, and mediastinal/tracheal shift direction to assess for right-sided volume loss.
actions.when: Options distinguish between right vs left pathology or attribute cause of shift/elevation.
actions.stop: Right hemidiaphragm is visibly elevated compared to the left AND mediastinum is shifted toward the right.

items.avoid: Misidentifying the scimitar vein as being on the left side or attributing the mediastinal shift to left lung hyperinflation; do not rely on automated reports that miss the subtle curved vascular shadow.
items.source_evidence: Old model predictions correctly identified the 'curved shadow near the right heart border' and 'right lung volume loss with right mediastinal shift and elevated right hemidiaphragm' as key features. Tool observations (report generator/classifier) failed to detect these specific signs, labeling the study limited or normal. The correction relies on direct visual confirmation of the right-sided anomalous vein and associated hypoplasia signs (elevated right diaphragm, ipsilateral shift), which are pathognomonic for scimitar syndrome.

items.topic: Longitudinal assessment of pulmonary edema resolution in aspiration

actions.observe: Inspect Figure 1 for bilateral perihilar fluffy opacities with peripheral sparing (bat-wing pattern) indicative of pulmonary edema/aspiration.
actions.when: Question asks to describe findings in the first image of a pair.
actions.stop: Perihilar opacities are identified and distinguished from focal consolidation or diffuse reticular patterns.

actions.observe: Compare Figure 2 lung fields against Figure 1 to verify complete clearance of opacities and restoration of normal vascular markings.
actions.when: Question requires assessing evolution or resolution between two timepoints.
actions.stop: Visual confirmation that Figure 2 lacks the opacities seen in Figure 1, supporting 'complete resolution' over 'partial resolution' or 'progression'.

items.avoid: Inferring severity changes from classifier score differences (e.g., 0.94 vs null); assuming 'no strong finding' implies normality without visual verification; misidentifying perihilar edema as lower lobe consolidation.
items.source_evidence: Old models correctly identified resolution but relied on classifier scores (0.94 opacity in Fig 1, none in Fig 2) which are uncalibrated. The correction confirms Figure 1 shows bilateral perihilar fluffy opacities (pulmonary edema) and Figure 2 shows complete resolution. Visual inspection is required to distinguish 'perihilar fluffy opacities' from 'lower lobe consolidation' or 'diffuse reticular opacities' and to confirm 'complete' rather than 'partial' resolution, as tool scores cannot quantify extent or pattern.

items.topic: COP radiographic pattern: peripheral middle/lower zone consolidation

actions.observe: Inspect lung parenchyma for patchy airspace opacities specifically located at the periphery (subpleural) of the middle and lower lung zones, sparing the upper zones and central hila.
actions.when: Question asks for diagnosis based on CXR pattern or describes consolidation distribution in a patient with subacute symptoms unresponsive to antibiotics.
actions.stop: Peripheral middle/lower zone consolidations are visually confirmed; do not rely on classifier scores which may miss this specific pattern.

actions.observe: Verify absence of dominant upper lobe cavitation, hilar lymphadenopathy, or diffuse reticular fibrosis to distinguish from TB, sarcoidosis, or IPF.
actions.when: Differentiating COP from other interstitial or granulomatous diseases based on distribution.
actions.stop: Pattern matches peripheral/basal predominance without upper lobe dominance or fibrotic honeycombing.

items.avoid: Trusting chest_xray_classifier 'no strong findings' or report generator 'no focal consolidation' outputs, as these tools frequently fail to detect the subtle, patchy peripheral opacities characteristic of COP. Do not assume normalcy from tool silence.
items.source_evidence: Old model predictions and tool observations (classifier/report generator) incorrectly suggested normal findings or failed to identify pathology. Released correct answers consistently identify 'Idiopathic Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP)' characterized by 'bilateral areas of airspace consolidation at the periphery of the middle and lower lung zones'. The visual evidence in Figure 1 confirms patchy opacities in these specific regions, contradicting the automated tool reports.

items.topic: Kartagener syndrome: dextrocardia and left-sided horizontal fissure (situs inversus)

actions.observe: Cardiac apex position relative to midline; confirm if pointing to patient's right (dextrocardia).
actions.when: Evaluating options involving heart orientation or situs inversus.
actions.stop: Apex clearly points to the right hemithorax.

actions.observe: Horizontal fissure location; verify if present in the left hemithorax (mirror image of normal right-sided fissure).
actions.when: Distinguishing between normal anatomy and situs inversus patterns.
actions.stop: Fissure is visualized on the left side, confirming mirror-image anatomy.

items.avoid: Relying on automated report generators that may default to 'normal cardiomediastinal silhouette' despite obvious dextrocardia; assuming bronchiectasis must be visible on CXR to diagnose Kartagener's when situs inversus is the primary radiographic clue.
items.source_evidence: Old models and tools frequently missed dextrocardia or misidentified fissure laterality. The chest_xray_report_generator incorrectly stated 'cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal' for a case with clear dextrocardia. Correct answers consistently link Kartagener syndrome to the combination of a right-sided heart apex and a left-sided horizontal fissure (situs inversus), supported by clinical history of sinusitis/infections. Visual inspection confirms the heart shadow is on the right and the horizontal fissure is on the left.

items.topic: Lung volume assessment with acquisition and field-of-view limitations

actions.observe: Assess visible diaphragm position/shape and available rib landmarks together with inspiration, projection and image coverage. State if those geometric cues cannot be judged from the supplied image.
actions.when: The current question explicitly asks about lung volume. Do not infer clinical physiology solely from a rib count or classifier score.
actions.stop: Stop when the visible volume cues and their acquisition limitations are identified; do not force an obstructive/restrictive diagnosis or a fixed rib-count threshold.

items.avoid: A cropped or poorly inspired image can mimic low volume. Plain-film geometry does not by itself establish a pulmonary-function diagnosis, and classifier magnitude is not a volume measurement.
items.source_evidence: Source9374 contains a frontal radiograph and feedback concerning lung-volume interpretation. Source review found that a rigid rib-count/physiology rule would overreach; this revision keeps only direct geometry and acquisition-limitation checks.
